paras: The lynching of Jennie Steer was the killing of a Black woman by a mob on the Beard plantation near Shreveport, Louisiana, in late July 1903. Accused of poisoning sixteen-year-old Lizzie Dolan with lemonade, Steer was pursued by a posse, hanged from a tree, and shot, while denying the charge to the end. Papers across the country carried the story, and two papers called it the first lynching of a Black woman in that part of the state or anywhere.

Lizzie Dolan was the daughter of John Dolan, described as a farmer of Caddo Parish and as a prominent planter near Shreveport. She died after drinking a glass of lemonade that, according to the Shreveport dispatch, Steer had poisoned; one syndicated item named the poison as strychnine and called Steer a servant. The dispatch said the poisoning "created intense excitement" in the neighborhood and that the girl "died in horrible agony," which "accentuated the rage of the mob."

According to the account a Picayune correspondent sent from Shreveport, Steer fled the Dolan household once the poisoning was known. A posse found her "crouching in a hay loft" and dragged her out when she refused to come down. Taken to the Dolan house, she was "fully identified" as the woman who had put poison in the lemonade, while she "indignantly denied" the crime.

The mob then led her to a nearby tree, put a rope around her neck, and again demanded a confession. She made none and was hanged, and while the body hung several bullets were fired into it by "enraged citizens." The wire placed the lynching about sundown on Saturday, July 25, on the Beard plantation near where the girl was poisoned.

Lizzie Dolan's funeral was held the next morning and, by the Picayune account, was attended by people "for miles around." The same account reported a "growing suspicion" that Steer had been involved in the unsolved murder of Mrs. Frank Matthews months earlier, a woman she had once served, and quoted Matthews's son as believing his mother had been killed by a woman. A later version added that all was quiet around Bayou La Chute and that there was "no apparent sympathy" for Steer among Black residents there.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or any official action against the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Most white papers ran the Shreveport dispatch nearly word for word from July 27, often under the attribution of a New Orleans Picayune special. The text called Steer "stubborn to the last" and said the proof against her was "direct and conclusive," a phrase the Savannah Morning News lifted into its headline. Mississippi weeklies printed the story under "LOUISIANA VENGEANCE" and "The Female Flend [Fiend]," while the Bossier Banner, in the neighboring parish, stated flatly that Steer "poisoned" the girl.

Some Northern papers were more guarded, writing that "it is charged" she gave the poison, and a Vermont roundup noted that she "protested her innocence to the last." Shorter news digests in Missouri, South Carolina, and Mississippi reduced it to a single line about a lynching for poisoning a white girl.

The Black press took the case up in early August. The St. Paul Appeal wrote that "the Southern cavaliers" had lynched a woman merely "charged" with poisoning, that there was "no proof," and that her body was riddled with bullets "by the superior Southern savages." Professional World headed its brief "Extra Legal Action" yet repeated that Steer had poisoned the girl, and the Seattle Republican entered her name in its July table of lynchings.

Accounts differ on timing: the Shreveport wire gave sundown Saturday, July 25, while the Bossier Banner said Sunday morning and Professional World said the lynching took place during the girl's funeral. Because the Picayune text places the funeral on the morning after the lynching, the Saturday date has the stronger support. One syndicated item also said Steer was captured "some distance away, at Bayou La Chute," rather than near the Dolan house, though the Bossier Banner placed the Beard plantation itself at Bayou La Chute.

reader.title: Lynching of Jennie Steer
bases: A mob hanged Jennie Steer from a tree and fired bullets into her body after a posse pursued and captured her on an accusation of poisoning (A2, A12, A19).

Every report says a mob hanged Steer and shot into the body with no officer or legal process mentioned (A1, A2, A12); the mob acted on the accusation that she had poisoned Lizzie Dolan and demanded a confession before hanging her (A2, A19).

The Picayune special/wire text (A1, A2, A5, A12), an independently worded Louisiana brief (A16), a differently detailed syndicated item (A17), and the Black press (A23, A25, A27) all report the lynching of Steer near Shreveport.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire / Picayune special
accounts.gist: Steer fled when the poisoning became known, was found in a hay loft by a posse, identified at the Dolan house, and hanged at sundown Saturday after refusing to confess; bullets were fired into the body. She denied the crime, but the dispatch called the proof 'direct and conclusive'.

accounts.label: Syndicated short version
accounts.gist: Investigation showed Lizzie Dolan had been poisoned with strychnine in lemonade given by a servant, Jennie Steer, who fled and was captured some distance away at Bayou La Chute and lynched.

accounts.label: Bossier Banner (neighboring parish)
accounts.gist: States as fact that Steer poisoned Lizzie Dolan on the Beard plantation, Bayou La Chute, and was lynched Sunday morning.

accounts.label: Black press
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Appeal said Steer was only 'charged', denied it, and was lynched with 'no proof'; Professional World said she was lynched while the victim's funeral was in progress.

framing.detail: The wire called the proof 'direct and conclusive' and the girl 'beautiful'; the Savannah Morning News headlined 'the Proof Against Her Was Conclusive', and Mississippi papers ran 'LOUISIANA VENGEANCE' and 'The Female Flend'.
Northern and Midwestern papers ran the Shreveport dispatch, some hedging with 'it is charged' or 'Charged With Poisoning' in the headline.
News digests reduced it to a line: lynched 'for poisoning a young white girl'; a Vermont roundup noted she 'protested her innocence to the last'.
The St. Paul Appeal mocked the 'Southern cavaliers' and 'superior Southern savages' and said there was 'no proof'.
Professional World headed the item 'Extra Legal Action' but repeated that Steer 'poisoned' the girl.
